---
title: "The switch statement: many cases, one question"
---

![The same dice program twice: on the left the if/else-if chain you know, on the right the new switch statement doing exactly the same job.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rstropek/ts-web-playground/main/exercises/0040-Switch/if-to-switch.png){width=620}

Look back at this part for a moment. The dice program picked one face
out of six with a chain of `===` comparisons. The hex exercise
translated the digit values 10 to 15 into the letters A to F with a
chain (@sec-hex). The rock-paper-scissors game turned the computer's
roll into a symbol, with a chain again (@sec-rps-computer). Three
programs share one shape, a single variable compared against one exact
value after another. Programmers meet this shape so often that
TypeScript has a statement built just for it: `switch`. This closing
chapter of the Conditions part teaches you nothing new to compute,
only a tidier way to write decisions you already make. And you'll
practice it on an old friend, the dice.

## AI tutor {#sec-tutor-switch}

The tutor of this part knows the switch statement too. If a case never
seems to run or a message comes out wrong, show the tutor your switch
and tell it what you rolled and what appeared.

## From chain to switch {#sec-switch-from-chain}

To have something concrete to rewrite, here is a small variant of the
dice program. It rolls the die exactly like the dice chapter
(@sec-floor), but instead of drawing a face, it prints the rolled
number as a German word:

```typescript
const dice: number = floor(random(1, 7));

let message: string;
if (dice === 1) { message = "Eins"; }
else if (dice === 2) { message = "Zwei"; }
else if (dice === 3) { message = "Drei"; }
else if (dice === 4) { message = "Vier"; }
else if (dice === 5) { message = "Fünf"; }
else { message = "Sechs"; }
```

Nothing in this chain is new: exact comparisons with `===`
(@sec-equality), a final `else` that is safe because `dice` can only
hold 1 to 6, and every branch with its braces, even on one line.

But read the chain out loud and you'll hear the repetition, "dice
equals, dice equals, dice equals", five times the same variable, five
times the same question. The **switch statement** says the repeated
part once:

```typescript
switch (dice) {
    case 1:
        message = "Eins";
        break;
    case 2:
        message = "Zwei";
        break;
    // ... the cases 3, 4, and 5 ...
    default:
        message = "Sechs";
        break;
}
```

Read it top to bottom:

- `switch (dice)` names the value to look at, once. Everything inside
  the braces asks questions about `dice`.
- Each **case** is one exact comparison: the line `case 3:` asks the
  same question as `dice === 3`. The computer walks the cases from top
  to bottom and jumps to the first one that matches.
- After the colon come the statements of that case, and `break` ends
  the case: leave the switch, continue after its closing brace.
- `default` is the case without a value. More about it below.

## break: the way out {#sec-switch-break}

A case does not end by itself. The `break` statement is what sends the
computer out of the switch, and forgetting it is the classic switch
mistake. Without a `break`, the computer finishes the case's
statements and simply keeps running, straight into the statements of
the *next* case, without asking whether that case matches. Programmers
say the execution *falls through*.

Play computer with it: delete the `break` after `message = "Eins";`
and roll a 1. The computer jumps to `case 1`, stores `"Eins"`, and
then, with no `break` to stop it, runs on into `case 2` and stores
`"Zwei"`. Only the `break` there ends the switch. The program shows
"Zwei" although it rolled a 1.

::: {.callout-warning}
## A sneaky bug
A missing `break` is not an error for TypeScript: the program runs,
there is no red squiggle, and the drawing simply shows the wrong
result. When a switch behaves strangely, check the ends of your cases
first, one `break` per case.
:::

## default: the else of the switch {#sec-switch-default}

The `default` case runs when no other case matched. That is exactly
the job the plain `else` did at the end of the chain: after five nos,
only the 6 is left, so the word dice can write `default` instead of
`case 6`. Like every case, the `default` ends with a `break`, so all
branches of the switch look the same.

The `default` case is optional. A switch without one is fine: when no
case matches, the switch simply does nothing, and the program
continues after the closing brace. You'll see both designs in this
chapter's exercises, one switch with a `default` and one without.

## When switch fits, and when it doesn't {#sec-switch-or-if}

A switch asks only one kind of question: "is the value exactly this?",
the `===` question. That makes it great for chains of exact cases, and
useless for everything else. A range like `mouseX < 100` from the
color areas cannot be a case, and neither can the `||` conditions of
the bouncing ball or the `&&` box tests of your games. Those decisions
stay with `if`.

Here's the rule of thumb. When you catch yourself writing three or more
`else if` lines that compare the *same* variable with `===`, the
chain is a switch candidate. The compared value doesn't have to be a
number, by the way: a switch can also ask about a string, with the
same character-for-character exactness you know from comparing
strings with `===`.

One more reason to learn the shape by heart: a similar `switch` exists
in C, Java, and C#, the languages your semicolon habit is already
preparing you for. Some languages grow the idea further. C# and
Rust, for example, offer more powerful variants that can match whole
patterns, not just single values. The shape you learn here is the
foundation for all of them.

## Your exercise: the dice in words {#sec-simple-dice-exercise}

The first exercise is the word dice from this chapter. The starter
code contains the finished `if`/`else if` chain; your job is to
replace it with a switch.

1. **Read the starter code.** Two small chores while you read: the
   starter rounds with `Math.floor`, a spelling you haven't met. It
   does the same as the `floor` you know, but this course always uses
   the p5.js helpers, so change it to `floor`. And the `dice`
   declaration is missing its data type; add `: number`, like every
   declaration in this course.
2. **Rewrite the chain as a switch**, one case at a time. Start with
   `switch (dice) {` and the case for the 1, run the program, and only
   then add the next case. One change, one run: exactness first.
3. **Turn the final else into the default.** The chain's last branch
   has no condition, and the switch's `default` is its twin.
4. **Test with forced rolls**, like you tested the dice faces
   (@sec-dice-exercise): replace the roll with `const dice: number = 1;`
   for a moment, check the word, and work through all six values. Then
   put the `random` line back.

{{< example https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rstropek/ts-web-playground/main/exercises/0040-Switch/simple-dice.yaml title="Simple dice" >}}

## Your exercise: the dice faces with switch {#sec-dice-switch-exercise}

The second exercise is a program you have already built once: the dice
with its six faces from the dice exercise (@sec-dice-exercise). The
roll, the anchors, and the `circle` calls all stay as they were; only
the decision around them changes from a chain to a switch. Get your
paper table of the nine anchor points out again; it is still the plan.

1. **Read the starter code.** The switch is started, and the cases for
   the 1 and the 2 are done. Compare the case for the 2 with your own
   dice solution: the `circle` calls are identical, only the frame
   around them changed. Add the missing `: number` to the `dice`
   declaration while you're there.
2. **Add the cases 3 to 6**, one at a time, with a `break` at the end
   of each. Your table tells you which anchors each face uses, and the
   reuse you found on paper still works: the 3 is the 2 plus the
   center, the 5 is the 4 plus the center.
3. **Write the 6 as a normal case.** This switch has no `default`,
   and it doesn't need one: `dice` always holds one of the six values,
   so one case per value covers every roll.
4. **Test with forced rolls**, face by face, against your paper table.
   Then restore the roll and enjoy a die that runs on a switch.

{{< example https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rstropek/ts-web-playground/main/exercises/0040-Switch/dice-switch.yaml title="Dice with switch" >}}

## For fast finishers: one more chain {#sec-switch-transfer}

One switch candidate from this part is still out there. The
rock-paper-scissors game translates the computer's roll into a symbol
with an `if`/`else if` chain (@sec-rps-computer), three exact cases on
one variable. Open your finished game and rewrite that chain as a
switch. The game must behave exactly as before, and you have a tester
who knows it well: you.
